$comment: How the USPA record tables map onto this project's categories.
The tables themselves are in `snapshots/uspa-records.json`, written by
`pnpm run data:crawl:records` and never edited by hand. That file says what the
federation publishes, in the federation's own words. This one says what those
words mean, and is the only half a person edits.
WHY THE POUND COLUMN GATES NOTHING, AND WHAT IT DOES INSTEAD
Every published record carries a kilogram figure and a pound figure. This file
used to say the two must never be compared, on the grounds that a cross-check
would fail the build weekly over rows whose kilogram figure was never in doubt.
That reasoning still holds against *gating* on the pound column and the gate is
still absent: no row is withheld for it, no figure is corrected from it, and
`columnCrossCheck.maximumDisagreements` below is set far above the observed
count so a meet weekend cannot trip it.
What replaced the silence is a second witness. Of 129,908 crawled rows, 5,271
print `0.00` pounds -- a blank cell, not a contradiction -- and 355 of the rows
this build publishes disagree with their own pound column by more than half a
kilogram, which is the smallest step any competition bar has. Those are not
rounding: they are a digit inserted into one cell, a decimal point moved, or a
weight-class figure pasted into the weight column, and the worst of them ship a
670 kg masters total whose own row says 147.7 lb.
The kilogram column still governs -- it is what the federation lifts to and what
every other part of this application works in -- so the kilogram figure is what
gets published. The pound figure is recorded alongside it as
`sourceDisagreement`, and the screen shows both and links to the table. A wrong
number a lifter can see is wrong is a different thing from a wrong number
presented with total confidence, and only the second one loses somebody a meet.

$comment: No digest, unlike the classification snapshot beside it.
A record is replaced every time somebody beats it, so this file changes after
every meet weekend. A digest that had to be re-cut weekly would stop being a
decision anybody made and become a step in a script -- and the unattended
refresh could not run at all without a human in the loop to re-cut it. What the
digest buys for the classification standards is bought here instead by the
checks below, which are about meaning rather than bytes: every value the
tables use has to be mapped, every mapping has to be used, and every table's
own title has to agree with the identifiers used to reach it.

$comment:book: The book has no identifier here: it is the federation's, `uspa` above.
Records are fetched by the federation the screen is already showing, so a second
name chosen in this file would be a second thing to keep in step with the first.
The failure is silent -- `recordArtifactId` would name files nobody asks for, and
the browser renders a lookup that finds nothing as "no records in this
category", which is a real answer for a category nobody has set a record in.
THE THREE MARGINS, AND WHY THERE ARE THREE
Item 6.3.3 puts every weight on the bar at a multiple of 2.5 kg and every jump
at 2.5 kg or more, and then says: "Exceptions to this rule are as follows".
The exceptions are the record rules. Item 6.3.4 asks a record attempt to be at
least 500 grams over the standing record, taken in the normal increasing
sequence, and 6.3.5 lets a lifter request a record attempt that is not a
multiple of 2.5 kg at all. Item 6.3.6 works the example: against a 100 kg
record, 100.0 / 101.0 / 101.5 / 102 are all legal. Item 8.1.5 states the
margin again from the records side. So `minimumIncrementKilograms` is 0.5, and
it is deliberately smaller than the loading increment -- rounding it up to a
round jump would undo the exemption it exists to express.
The closing paragraphs of Part 8 carve out the other two cases.
First: "A lifter requesting to set a new record at a meet that is at a sanction
level less than the one they are competing in (i.e. requesting to break a State
Record at the National Championships), may only do so by using 2.5 kilo
increments (not 500 grams) and must break the current record by at least 2.5
kilos." The same paragraph confirms the ordinary case both ways round: a
National or World record may be taken with 500 grams at the National
Championships, and the World record may be taken with 500 grams at IPL Worlds,
while a State or National record at IPL Worlds needs 2.5 kilos. So
`higherSanctionIncrementKilograms` is 2.5.
In one sentence: chip by 500 grams when the record being claimed is at the
meet's level or above it, and add the full 2.5 kilos when the record is below
the meet's level. Note the "or above": a lifter at a state meet sanctioned to
allow the claim takes a National record with 500 grams too. Only a record
beneath the meet costs the full increment, and that direction is the half of
the rule that gets written backwards.
The chip is measured from the record as published, never from the next 2.5
kilo bar multiple above it -- a 200.5 kilo record is taken at 201, not 202.5.
That is the whole point of 6.3.5's exemption.
The full increment is not the mirror of that, and this is the part worth
reading twice. The paragraph withdrawing the 500 gram allowance is the same
paragraph imposing the 2.5 kilo margin -- "may only do so by using 2.5 kilo
increments (not 500 grams) and must break the current record by at least 2.5
kilos" -- so both conditions bind at once, and without 6.3.5 the bar is back
under 6.3.3's multiple-of-2.5 rule. Against that 200.5 kilo record a level
down, 203 clears the margin but cannot be loaded, and 202.5 can be loaded but
clears the record by 2. The answer is 205: the first ordinary multiple at or
above the record plus the full increment. Both of the simpler arithmetics get
it wrong, and both cost the lifter the record rather than merely an attempt.
One field carries both conditions because the rulebook states both with the
same number in the same sentence. About 6.6% of the published rows are not
multiples of 2.5, so this is one record in fifteen and not a curiosity.
Nothing in this file says which level outranks which, and nothing needs to. The
condition is the sanction level of the meet the lifter has entered, which this
project does not ask for and could not check. Both figures are published and
each is labelled with when it holds; the lifter knows which meet they are at.
Second: "Lifters attempting to set a new National or World Record that was
established with a minimum standard and is not an actual existing National or
World Record with a name and date, may do so by either matching or breaking the
minimum standard." Item 8.1.11.1 says the same thing from the other side --
"`Preset Records' are not established records; they are minimum numbers
required to replace the Preset Record with an actual record." Those are exactly
the rows `placeholderHolders` below marks as unclaimed, so
`matchTakesUnclaimedLevelIds` names the two levels the rule names and no
others. State is left out because the rulebook leaves it out: a lifter told to
match a figure the rules ask them to beat loses the record on the platform,
which is the more expensive of the two mistakes.
$comment:tableUrl: Where one published table lives, so a lifter can read a record where the
There is no certificate to link to. The federation publishes none, and the crawl
carries no per-record address, so a link claiming to be one would resolve to
nothing or -- worse -- to somebody else's record. What exists is this page, which
is one level, one drug-tested status and one event: the same three identifiers
the crawler walks the index for.
The crawler reads this template too, rather than building the address itself.
Two copies would be a link that rots the day the site moves and a build that
never notices, because a build never follows a link. Shared, the drift fails the
$comment:locations: Each link on the records site, and the level and region it stands for.
`titleLevel` and `titleRegion` are the segments the table's own heading uses. The
heading is the only thing a downloaded table says about which table it is, which
makes it the one cross-check available against the three identifiers used to
reach it -- and a stale link on the records site, filing one state's records
under another state's name, is otherwise invisible: plausible figures, in the
wrong place, with nothing on screen to say so.
`regionId` is `null` for a level the catalogue gives no regions to. It is not a
shorthand for "all regions": the browser builds its request from a level and a
region the lifter picked, so a record filed under a level with no region would
be unreachable under a level that has them.
$comment:statuses: The federation keeps two separate books, and a record in one says nothing about
the other. `tested` is part of a record's scope for that reason, not a filter.
$comment:events: One published event is one discipline in one equipment category.
`equipmentId` comes from the event and never from `titleGear`, which is wrong for
exactly one event: `classic-powerlifting` is headed `Raw`, and reading the
heading would file every classic raw record in the country under raw. The gear
segment is carried anyway because the heading cross-check needs it whole.
A federation that added a strict-curl book would add a line here and a discipline
to the categories document; the build refuses an event nothing maps, so it cannot
arrive as a silently missing set of records.
$comment:lifts: `TOTAL` is the three-lift total and only a full-power event holds one. A row
whose lift the event's discipline does not contest is dropped rather than
published -- see `plausibility` for why that is a rule and not a list.
$comment:divisions: The tables name a sex and an age division in one string, so both are read from
it. Thirty-six lines for eighteen divisions: the two sexes are spelled
differently and neither can be derived from the other by rule.
`15 TO 19` overlaps `16 TO 17` and `18 TO 19`, and that is the federation's own
arrangement rather than a transcription mistake -- the categories document
carries `junior-15-19` for it. Collapsing the three would drop more than a
thousand live records, some of them current world records.
$comment:weightClasses: Keyed by sex as well as by column, because the two ladders share numbers: `52kg`
is a women's class and a men's class and they are different records.
$comment:unmappedWeightClasses: Columns the tables print that the rulebook's ladders do not contain.
Every one of them is on the IPL world tables and nowhere else, and every one is a
column from the other sex's ladder appearing under this one. The largest, women's
`140+kg/SHW`, holds 255 rows of which 111 are byte-identical copies of the row
above them and 144 carry men's figures. These are an artefact of how that one
template is rendered, not a division anybody competed in.
Listed rather than left to fail, and listed by rule rather than by row: the whole
column is refused, so a meet that adds a record to one of them next month does
not break the unattended refresh. 343 rows of 129,908 when curated.
That count, and the per-column counts below, are what the tables held on the day
and are deliberately not in the `reason` strings. A reason is printed once per
withheld row and read by whoever is looking at a build, so a figure inside one
goes stale the first weekend somebody sets a record -- and it reads as a
contradiction long before anybody thinks to check it, because the build prints
the real count beside it. Per column when curated: 125kg/275lb 14, 140kg/308.5lb

$comment:absentLocations: Places the records site links to and the table service does not answer for.
Recorded here rather than in the categories document, because the absence is a
fact about the records service and not about who may compete. Guam is a USPA
region; it simply has no record tables configured, and every one of its twenty
links answers 503 immediately and every time.
Checked both ways. A location listed here that starts answering is a failed
build, because the alternative is a region whose records are silently never
published; and a location that stops answering without being listed is a failed
build too, because that is what a state's records disappearing looks like.

absentLocations.reason: Linked from the records index, but every one of its tables answers 503. No records have been configured for it.

$comment:placeholderHolders: Holder cells that name no lifter.
The USPA seeded its record book by writing a figure into every category so the
first lifter in one had something to beat, and put "Record Preset" in the
holder column to say so. Nearly thirteen thousand of the hundred and thirty
thousand published rows are these -- a tenth of the corpus -- almost all
stamped 04/10/2011 or 23/10/2010, the days the book was founded, and many
carrying a pound figure of 0.00.
A seeded figure is a real record to a lifter: clearing it takes the record.
What it is not is a lift somebody made, so the holder and the date are dropped
and the published record is flagged `unclaimed` instead. Printing "Record
Preset" as a name is the version that shipped first, and it reads as a person.
Here rather than in the adapter so the day the federation changes the wording
the fix is a mapping edit and a data refresh rather than a release. Matched
case-insensitively: these tables are hand-maintained across fifty-odd pages,
and an unmatched variant is published as a lifter with several thousand
records and nothing on screen to say otherwise.
Checked one way only. A mapped placeholder that appears in no row fails the
build, because a renamed placeholder is exactly what that looks like. The
other direction cannot be checked at all -- a placeholder nobody mapped is
indistinguishable from a lifter, which is the whole reason a stale entry here
is worth a failed build.

placeholderHolders.reason: The federation's own seeded figure for a category nobody has claimed. Dated to the founding of the record book, not to a lift.

$comment:plausibility: The rules that decide which published rows are not published onward.
Rules, never a list of rows. A row-listed quarantine is what the classification
standards use, and it works there because that dataset is a fixed table somebody
re-exports by hand. These tables change after every meet weekend and refresh
without a human, so a list would go stale between Sunday and Monday and stop the
refresh on a row nobody had had a chance to look at.
Three rules drop 399 of 129,908 rows, 0.31%: 343 in a weight class the sex's
ladder does not contain (above), 36 in a lift the event's discipline does not
contest -- a deadlift printed on a bench-only table -- and 20 outside the band
below.
The band is set wide enough to be about parsing rather than about performance.
The heaviest real single lift in the corpus is 545 kg and the heaviest real total
1,241.1 kg; the lightest real lift is 20 kg, which is a bare bar and belongs to a
ten-year-old. Nothing genuine is near these edges, and a figure that is means the
column moved or a decimal point did.
`maximumExcludedRows` is the part that earns its keep. Every rule above is a rule
a parser regression could satisfy for thousands of rows at once -- a shifted
column makes every weight class unrecognisable -- and the result would be a
successful build publishing a fraction of the records with nothing said. 600
against today's 399 is room for a federation adding a class or a template, and
far below the first digit of a real failure.
$comment:columnCrossCheck: Reading the pound column back as a second witness to the kilogram column. The
header explains why this records a disagreement instead of gating on one.
`poundsPerKilogram` is the federation's own displayed factor, truncated the way
the federation truncates it, and it lives here rather than in code because it is
a property of this federation's arithmetic and not of the SI definition. Using
the exact factor instead would put roughly a thousand extra rows over the
tolerance for no reason but the fourth decimal place.
`toleranceKilograms` is half a kilogram: the smallest step a competition bar can
be loaded to, so a disagreement below it cannot describe a different lift. The
distribution says the same thing -- 124,110 of 124,637 comparable rows land
inside it, and the closest exceedance is a pound cell truncated to a whole pound
(227.5 kg printed as 501 lb, which is 227.25).
`maximumDisagreements` is the redesign detector, and it is the only part of this
block that can fail a build. If the pound column moves one place left, every row
disagrees at once and the corpus would otherwise publish 129,509 records each
carrying a bogus second figure. 900 against today's 355 leaves room for a heavy
meet season without leaving room for that.
